name: Radical democracy
summary: Radical democracy, in the contemporary post-structuralist sense of Laclau, Mouffe, Ranciere and others, holds that democracy is deepened by extending equality and liberty to ever more social relations and by keeping political conflict alive, since a final rational consensus is impossible. It treats social orders as contingent products of hegemonic struggle, rejects class essentialism and natural titles to rule, and distrusts the post-political consensus of the centre.
scope: The poststructuralist family of Laclau and Mouffe (Hegemony and Socialist Strategy, agonistic pluralism, left populism), with Ranciere, Lefort, Abensour and Butler as scholarship counts them (Sanchez Santiago). Mouffe's texts carry most answers. It excludes the older 'radical democracy' of Rousseau, participatory-democracy and deliberative strands such as Habermas's, which the scholarship no longer groups with it, and the Marxist tradition. No state applied it, so there is no record beyond its theorists' words.

democracy-needs-political-clash.rationale: Mouffe calls agonistic confrontation 'the very condition of existence' of democracy and says a well-functioning democracy calls for a vibrant clash of democratic positions; Sanchez Santiago (section 5.3) lists the revaluation of conflict as one of the family's three shared traits.

democracy-best.rationale: The project is to deepen and radicalise democracy, whose principles of liberty and equality Mouffe says should be taken literally and held to account, and the sources never set a limit on the people's say.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Mouffe says that in 'post-democratic' societies democracy is spoken of only to mean universal suffrage and majority rule while equality and popular sovereignty are given up, so competitive elections alone do not make a democracy.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Modern democracy's specificity lies in recognising and legitimating conflict and refusing to suppress it with an authoritarian order, and the adversary's right to defend his or her ideas is never questioned.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Sanchez Santiago defines the approach by direct, active citizen participation in all spheres of social life and a more demanding citizenship involving everyone in the res publica; Mouffe blames the discouragement of active involvement for democratic disaffection.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Sanchez Santiago describes labour struggles as making the factory and the work contract a collective matter open to public deliberation and legislative regulation, part of extending equality to spheres still ruled by hierarchy; the sources do not discuss a vote on company management specifically.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Sanchez Santiago presents feminist struggles over the public/private line and the push to impose equality in spheres such as the family, which radical democrats treat as political, but does not discuss marital authority by name.

experts-over-public.rationale: Mouffe attacks post-politics for turning politics into a technical matter reserved for experts, and Sanchez Santiago says democracy is the power of anyone, the government of the 'incompetents' who lack natural or acquired titles to rule.

natural-rulers.rationale: Under radical democracy no one has a natural right to command by greater wisdom, wealth, force or lineage, and no one is bound to obey for lacking these qualities (Sanchez Santiago, section 5.1, drawing on Ranciere).

dynastic-succession.rationale: The same section denies any natural title to command by lineage, which a hereditary succession to a leader's office contradicts.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Following Lefort, democracy 'disincorporates' power, which in old monarchies was embodied in the prince; a sacred ruler is the opposite arrangement.

elective-rulers.rationale: Democracy makes power the object of a regulated periodic contest rather than the natural property of a person or group (Lefort as set out by Sanchez Santiago); Mouffe's whole case is for electoral confrontation between rival projects.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Sanchez Santiago, following Lefort, contrasts democracy with regimes where a leader or party places itself above the laws and is the sole source of norms; in democracy law and power can be questioned by anyone.

leader-cult.rationale: A leader or party that incarnates the nation is, in Lefort's account set out by Sanchez Santiago, the mark of totalitarian regimes that democracy's 'empty place of power' excludes.

one-party-rule.rationale: Rule by a single party that monopolises power and knowledge is described as the totalitarian opposite of democracy, and Mouffe's agonism needs competing parties and projects.

total-state.rationale: Lefort's totalitarian regime, in which one body seizes all power and knowledge, is the counter-model of democracy, and Abensour and Ranciere treat the state as an apparatus of unifying coercion.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Mouffe describes financialised capitalism as producing a growing 'oligarchization' of Western societies in which popular sovereignty and equality are lost; Sanchez Santiago adds Rousseau's test that no citizen be rich enough to buy another.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Radical democracy extends the demand for equality and liberty for all individuals to every sphere of social life; Mouffe names 'liberty and equality' as the ethico-political principles all adversaries share.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Mouffe says the authority of political institutions is 'not a question of consent' but of continuing acknowledgement by citizens, and that legitimacy has no a priori ground, while also making popular sovereignty a core democratic principle; the sources pull both ways.

separated-powers.rationale: Mouffe treats the rule of law and separation of powers as the liberal half of liberal democracy, whose tension with the democratic half she wants kept alive rather than resolved.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Mouffe holds that liberal institutions protect individual freedom against the tyranny of the majority and are necessary once homogeneity is given up (as quoted by Le Goff from The Return of the Political), so a majority is not left unconstrained.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Mouffe says the post-political claim that left and right are obsolete denies the we/they frontier politics always needs, and she criticises Third Way attempts to combine the two as entrenching the existing hegemony.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Mouffe condemns post-politics for reducing politics to a technical matter of managing the established order and insists that politics is partisan, with no neutral ground.

single-common-good.rationale: Mouffe says there can be no rational consensus on one common good: each political project proposes its own interpretation of the common good and a different hegemony, and the clash among them is the substance of democracy.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Mouffe argues that democratic allegiance rests on passions, collective affects and forms of life rather than on rational justification, and that politics cannot be understood without the role of affects.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Sanchez Santiago says radical democrats refuse to ground democratic politics in human nature or other last foundations, and Mouffe criticises the liberal picture of individuals prior to society as bearers of natural rights.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Mouffe holds that social objectivity is constituted by acts of power and bears the traces of exclusion, and that the ground of hegemonic struggle is never neutral; she does not discuss scientific knowledge as such.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Laclau and Mouffe reject the ontological centrality of the working class and class-based history, and Mouffe's agonistic struggle between adversaries takes the place of class struggle.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Radical democrats reject grounding the social order ontologically in economic and class relations and treat every social order as the contingent product of hegemonic political practices.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The central concept of hegemony holds that an order rests on a pattern of power that has won recognition as legitimate and appears natural; Sanchez Santiago says the current moment is one of Gramscian wars of position.

political-decisions-consensus.rationale: Mouffe says a rational consensus without exclusion cannot exist, every decision excludes alternatives, and too much emphasis on consensus breeds apathy and the rise of antagonisms.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Mouffe describes the ethno-nationalist construction of 'the people' that excludes immigrants as a non-progressive, xenophobic form, and calls for a different, equality-based construction of the people.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Mouffe endorses Oakeshott's view that citizens recognise an obligation to obey the conditions of the res publica, which counts against a view that there is no general duty to obey the law.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Le Goff reports that Mouffe's Towards a Green Democratic Revolution calls for a break with the neoliberal order and for confronting the power of fossil capital to meet the ecological emergency.

parliamentary-road-socialism.rationale: Mouffe, as quoted by Le Goff, holds that socialist goals can only be achieved acceptably within the liberal democratic framework, which she wants to radicalise rather than leave.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Mouffe and Laclau want to democratise liberal institutions from within, while Abensour and Ranciere set democracy against the state and its institutions (Sanchez Santiago, section 5.2); the sources do not say any strand wants the state machinery replaced.

direct-action.rationale: Sanchez Santiago contrasts the 'Ranciere moment' of disruptive action against institutions with today's Gramscian wars of position inside state institutions, and Mouffe campaigns for electoral politics; the sources show a split.

political-violence-never.rationale: The sources distinguish adversaries from enemies but state no position on whether political violence is ever justified.

multipolar-world.rationale: Mouffe argues the need for a multipolar world order of several large regional units coexisting, each with its own forms of democracy, in place of one dominant power.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Mouffe says imposing the Western conception of democracy as the only legitimate one on reluctant societies breeds antagonism between civilizations, and that liberal democracy is only one form of democracy among others.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Mouffe holds that a plurality of just forms of society and of democracy must be recognised as legitimate, so Western institutions need not be adopted everywhere.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Mouffe defends value pluralism and the legitimacy of a plurality of forms of society, and denies societies the right to rank cultures and impose one model, though she does not state the equality claim in these words.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Mouffe treats the universal enforcement of the Western version of human rights as a hegemonic imposition that provokes violent reaction, and she wants international institutions that allow pluralism.

universal-morality.rationale: Mouffe calls for a world order that acknowledges value pluralism in the strong Weberian and Nietzschean sense and rejects a 'Reign of Reason' from which one rational morality would rule all cultures.

missingStatements.text: People's political identities are formed by political action.
missingStatements.rationale: Mouffe holds that politics constitutes identities instead of representing ready-made ones, and that there are no essential identities, only forms of identification.

quotes.text: political practice cannot be envisaged in simply representing the interests of pre-constituted identities, but in constituting those identities themselves in a precarious and always vulnerable terrain
quotes.where: mouffe.txt, section An Agonistic Model of Democracy, p.14

quotes.text: there are no essential identities but only forms of identification. What is at stake in politics is the construction of political identities
quotes.where: affects.txt, The Affects of Democracy, p.63

missingStatements.text: Democratic politics should mobilise people's collective passions.
missingStatements.rationale: Mouffe calls the mobilisation of passions towards democratic designs the prime task of democratic politics, against the rationalist aim of excluding them.

quotes.text: the prime task of democratic politics is not to eliminate passions from the sphere of the public, in order to render a rational consensus possible, but to mobilize those passions towards democratic designs
quotes.where: mouffe.txt, section An Agonistic Model of Democracy, p.16

quotes.text: an affect can only be displaced by an opposed affect, stronger than the one to be repressed

notes: Themes searched in Mouffe's 2000 paper and 2018 lecture, Sanchez Santiago's 2024 entry and Le Goff's 2024 review, plus Dahlberg (2011) on digital radical democracy and the SEP Democracy entry (neither states positions beyond participation and counter-publics): institutions, elections, courts, executive power, conflict, passions, populism, identity, class, capitalism, ecology, family, immigration and nation, war and international order. The record is almost silent on economics (taxes, ownership, welfare), foreign policy and war, criminal justice, religion, technology and most social questions, so those are null. The strand splits on direct action and on how far to keep liberal institutions. Mouffe's multipolar-world paper (CIDOB 2010) supplied the foreign-policy positions. Hegemony and Socialist Strategy and Mouffe's later books (For a Left Populism, Towards a Green Democratic Revolution, The Democratic Paradox) were not available in full text; only the review's quotations were used.
